blocks.stub_fs: School cleaning standards are the hygiene and amenity requirements a school keeps across classrooms, toilets, corridors and canteens.
blocks.answer: School cleaning standards are **the hygiene and amenity requirements a school keeps across classrooms, toilets, corridors and canteens** – the duties a school documents and a contractor delivers on schedule.
before: In Victoria the frame is practical rather than a single statute. The Department of Education sets the environment a state school must maintain, the school's own brief turns that environment into named tasks and the contractor delivers against both. A cleaner inside a school is not doing office work with children nearby – the areas, the hours and the safety rules are all different.
The standards a business manager writes down answer three questions:

items.text: which surfaces carry germ risk between students and how often each is treated.
whether toilets, corridors and shared rooms stay usable through the day.
which records prove the work ran, so a complaint or inspection has an answer.

after: Classrooms sit at the centre of the frame because every student passes through them daily. The rest of the campus – canteens, gyms, admin – hangs off the same requirement structure at different intensities.

blocks.stub_fs: The requirements come from Department of Education guidance, the school's own spec and public health advice.
blocks.answer: The requirements come from **Department of Education guidance, the school's own spec and public health advice** – three layers that stack, not one document.

items.text: the department's facilities expectations: safe buildings, usable amenities and hygienic shared spaces.
the campus's own task list: rooms, frequencies, products and the sign-off chain the principal's office keeps.
outbreak and hygiene guidance that changes with seasons and events.
the requirement that lands in the cleaner's agreement; everything above collapses into clauses the contractor must meet.

after: A spec that names rooms without frequencies fails in practice – the cleaner cannot tell "daily" from "when it looks dirty", and the business manager cannot audit what was never specified. The public health layer is the one that moves: a gastro outbreak or flu season lifts disinfection frequency in writing, not just in spirit.

blocks.h2: The areas a school clean covers
blocks.stub_fs: A school clean covers classrooms, amenities blocks, corridors, gym floors, canteens and admin zones.
blocks.answer: A school clean covers **classrooms, amenities blocks, corridors, gym floors, canteens and admin zones** – each with its own frequency and product rules.

items.text: desks, chair tops, teacher surfaces and floor areas; the highest-volume zone on campus.
student toilets, basins, dispensers and urinals; the zone with the strictest hygiene line.
floors, handrails and lockers; traffic areas that collect soil all day.
sports courts and equipment rooms; dust, sweat marks and floor-finish care.
food-service surfaces, sinks and floors; cleaning rules closer to a kitchen than a classroom.
office desks, reception and staff rooms; standard office duties at school hours.

after: The zone map decides the roster. A campus where the amenities block sits far from the classrooms needs its own run between recess blocks – geography is a scheduling fact, not a detail.

Each area also carries a different product rule. Canteen surfaces need food-safe product; amenities blocks need a proper disinfectant cycle; gym floors take a dust-mop and occasional wet pass so the floor finish survives the term. Writing the product against the area is what turns a task list into a deliverable.

Keeping the school clean is the zone map plus the between-visit layer: the evening pass resets every zone on this list, while staff and students keep classrooms and canteen tidy during the day – the duty list owns the zones, the school owns the habits between visits.

blocks.h2: The duties a school cleaner carries
blocks.stub_fs: A school cleaner's duties run vacuum, mop, sanitise amenities, empty bins and wipe touch points in a set zone order.
blocks.answer: A school cleaner's duties run **vacuum, mop, sanitise amenities, empty bins and wipe touch points** in a set zone order. Responsibilities extend past the mop: the cleaner is the person who sees the campus at its emptiest, so the role quietly absorbs reporting duties too.
before: The task set the task list names:

items.text: cleanest to dirtiest: teaching rooms and admin first, amenities blocks last, so a cloth never travels backwards.
room bins emptied, relined and moved to the collection point on the school's waste day.
door furniture, railings, switches and shared equipment wiped on the daily pass.
damage, graffiti and spills beyond routine scope logged for the business manager's morning review.

after: Duties split by day part as well. The after-hours crew runs the deep loop; a day porter – where the school pays for one – handles spills, amenities top-ups and event resets while classes run.

The responsibilities list extends into the audit trail. A school cleaner's signature on the rota is the evidence the duty ran; a missed signature reads as a missed visit even when the floor is spotless. A school that treats the log as optional discovers at complaint time that the work was invisible.

The duties also answer the mistake-and-output questions the same way: the task list prevents the seven errors campuses see most – dusting before wiping, skipping touch points, cloths travelling from amenities back to classrooms, ignoring edges, over-wetting gym floors, mixing chemicals and unrelined bins – and it measures a cleaner's two or three hours as a named slice of the zone order, not a guess.

blocks.h2: What are the 6 basic cleaning steps in a school?
blocks.stub_fs: The six steps run wash, wipe, rinse, dry, check and sign.
blocks.answer: The six steps run **wash, wipe, rinse, dry, check and sign** – the same surface loop every zone repeats.

items.text: detergent lifts soil; skipping this step locks dirt under disinfectant.
the disinfectant pass, contact time observed.
residue removed on food-contact and desk surfaces.
moisture removed so the next treatment is not diluted.
a visual pass against the spec line for that zone.
the rota entry that turns the pass into evidence.

after: The five basic cleaning principles underneath the loop are fixed too: clean top-down, work clean-to-dirty, match the product to the surface, observe contact time, and verify before moving on – the "seven stages" some schedules quote just split the same loop into preparation, dust, wash, disinfect, rinse, dry and check. A spec that names the loop and the principles underneath it leaves nothing to the cleaner's memory.

blocks.h2: Do janitors clean classrooms every day?
blocks.stub_fs: Yes – janitors clean classrooms every school day, typically after hours.
blocks.answer: **Yes – janitors clean classrooms every school day**, typically after hours once students and staff have left.
before: The daily pass covers vacuum or sweep, desk tops, bins and touch points; disinfection of high-touch surfaces sits on the same loop or doubles up during illness season. Between-visit tidiness stays with the class – the cleaner resets the room, the students keep it that way until the next pass.

blocks.h2: What is a cleaner at a school called?
blocks.stub_fs: A school cleaner is called a cleaner, custodian or facilities officer.
blocks.answer: A school cleaner is called a **cleaner, custodian or facilities officer** – the title changes, the duty set does not.
before: Cleaner title variants matter mainly for the brief: the position description may read custodian or grounds staff, but the contract clause names the tasks either way. Facilities officer usually signals extra duties – deliveries, setups and basic maintenance – wrapped around the cleaning core.

blocks.h2: How many hours does a school need per week?
blocks.stub_fs: A school's weekly hours are set by enrolment and building size – the roster is specified per zone.
blocks.answer: A school's weekly hours are **set by enrolment and building size** – the roster is specified per zone, not bought as a lump; a service provider prices against that roster.
before: Weekly hours scale on three drivers: enrolment sets traffic, building size sets floor area and the zone mix sets intensity – amenities blocks and canteens cost more per square metre than classrooms. A campus of a few hundred students runs a smaller crew than a multi-building secondary college, and the duty list should say so in writing.

Hours also flex across the year. Term breaks absorb the deep cleans the school fortnight cannot fit; event weeks add gym and hall resets; wet weather pushes mud through every entry and lifts corridor passes. A roster priced only for the quiet weeks fails the messy ones.

The same section answers the hourly question from the other side: a "good cleaner per hour" is priced inside the roster figure – the school buys zones per week, and the hourly number never reaches the invoice. Asking the provider to size the roster against the zone list is the only honest rate comparison a buyer gets.

blocks.h2: How does a school stay clean between visits?
blocks.stub_fs: A school stays clean between visits through tidy routines, lunch supervision, waste systems and spill reporting.
blocks.answer: A school stays clean between visits through **tidy routines, lunch supervision, waste systems and spill reporting** – the housekeeping layer students and staff own.

items.text: teaching rooms end the day with chairs up and floors clear so the evening pass reaches every surface.
yard duty keeps food waste inside eating zones instead of corridors.
enough bins, emptied before they overflow, placed where students actually use them.
a named person who hears about a spill or mess before it becomes a hazard.

after: Ten small habits beat one heroic clean: the between-visit layer is what makes the evening pass a maintenance job rather than a rescue – and it costs nothing but routine.

Household-style cleaning rules read as between-visit habits on a school: the "one-hour rule" is the tidy-window the day porter owns, the "20/10" rhythm of working in short bursts maps to recess-length resets, and the twenty-minute touch-up loop is what lunch supervision does for eating zones. The roster absorbs all of them – a rule is just a roster someone never wrote down.

blocks.h2: What questions do business managers ask?
blocks.stub_fs: The questions business managers ask before scoping a program.
blocks.answer: The buying conversation lands on a short list – the spec, the site walk and the quote settle the questions each one raises:

qa.q: What are the recommended guidelines for school cleaning?
qa.a: For business managers the answer is the school's own duty list – areas, frequencies, products and sign-off – built on Department of Education guidance and current health advice.

qa.q: What are the duties of a school cleaner?
qa.a: Vacuum, mop, sanitise amenities, empty bins and wipe touch points in zone order, plus damage and spill reporting.

qa.q: What is a cleaner at a school called?
qa.a: Cleaner, custodian or facilities officer – the tasks are defined by the spec, not the title.

qa.q: Do janitors clean classrooms every day?
qa.a: Yes – every school day, typically after hours, with touch-point disinfection on the same loop.

qa.q: What are the 6 basic cleaning steps?
qa.a: Wash, wipe, rinse, dry, check and sign – the surface loop every zone repeats.

qa.q: What is the 1 minute rule for cleaning?
qa.a: If a task takes under a minute – a spill, a dropped wrapper, a smear on glass – do it now rather than logging it; on a school rota the day porter owns that window.

qa.q: What is the 5-5-5 rule for cleaning?
qa.a: A declutter habit that sorts a room into keep, donate and remove – useful for storerooms and lost-property shelves, while the spec names the clutter zones everywhere else.
